chunks.text: 3 Materials and method 3.1 Datasets The pre-training dataset comprised 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans pooled from multiple studies within the iSTAGING consortium Habes et al. (2021) . While the majority of scans were from cognitively unimpaired subjects, the dataset also included individuals with MCI and dementia, enabling the model to capture disease-related neuroanatomical changes. We expect that including diseased groups in pre-training plays a beneficial role in downstream tasks presented in Section 4 for disease classification. A detailed breakdown of pre-training datasets and sample characteristics is provided in Table 1 . The dataset was stratified by diagnosis and partitioned into 80% training, 10% validation and 10% test set at the participant level, so that all longitudinal scans from a given participant were assigned to the same set. To ensure a balanced age distribution across splits, scans were stratified into 10-year age bins and partitioned into 60% for training, 30% for validation, and 10% for testing. We removed subjects aged ≤ 40 \leq 40 , resulting in a total of n = 363 n=363 , reflecting the clinical scope of the model where neurodegeneration-related structural changes are most relevant. All scans underwent the same preprocessing pipeline as with Brain2Vec pre-training introduced in Sec. 3.3 , including skull-stripping, atlas registration, resampling to 128 × 128 × 128 128\times 128\times 128 voxels and Z-score normalization. 3.2 Architecture Figure 1 : Overview of the Brain2Vec pre-training architecture and downstream applications. (Pre-training) Brain2Vec is a 3D Masked Autoencoder (MAE) pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans from the iSTAGING consortium. Input volumes are divided into 8 × 8 × 8 8\times 8\times 8 patches, with 75% randomly masked. A 12-layer Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder processes only the visible patches to generate a 768-dimensional latent representation. Mask tokens are then introduced, and an 8-layer ViT decoder reconstructs the original scan. (Evaluation) The pre-trained encoder serves two complementary roles. First, it provides a robust weight initialization for end-to-end fine-tuning on a downstream task (brain age regression), accelerating convergence and improving accuracy relative to random initialization. Second, its frozen 768-dimensional embeddings serve as fixed features for lightweight downstream models, including a Support Vector Regressor (SVR) for brain age regression and SVMs for five binary classification tasks: CU vs. AD, elevated BMI, diabetes, smoking status, and hypertension. We additionally assess the quality and interpretability of these frozen embeddings via self-attention visualization, correlation with anatomically-defined Regions of Interest (ROIs), and latent-space manipulation, showing that Brain2Vec encodes spatially localized, neuroanatomically meaningful representations. Brain2Vec is a 3D Masked Autoencoder He et al. (2022) with an assymetric encoder-decoder design (Fig. 1 ). Feature extraction.

A preprocessed volume x ∈ ℝ 128 × 128 × 128 x\in\mathbb{R}^{128\times 128\times 128} is split into N = 16 3 = 4096 N=16^{3}=4096 non-overlapping 8 × 8 × 8 8\times 8\times 8 patches { x p } p = 1 N \{x_{p}\}_{p=1}^{N} , each flattened to a 512-dimensional vector and linearly projected to the encoder width d = 768 d=768 . A learnable [CLS] token is prepended to the sequence. Tokenization. The encoder is a 12-layer ViT Dosovitskiy et al. (2020) with a hidden size of 768, 12 attention heads, and an MLP ratio of 4. A random subset (75%) of patches are masked and the encoder only processes a small subset of visible patches (25%), without incorporating mask tokens Devlin et al. (2019) . Decoder. The decoder is an 8-layer ViT with an input dimensionality of d = 512 d=512 and 16 attention heads. The encoder’s outputs are first projected to the required dimensionality and a shared learnable mask token is inserted at every masked position, followed by positional embeddings. The decoder processes the full sequence of tokens and a linear head predicts the 8 × 8 × 8 = 512 8\times 8\times 8=512 voxel values of each patch. In all previous work, the decoder is not used for feature extraction but only during pre-training and discarded afterwards. We proposed an approach on using the decoder for interpretability (Sec. 4.3 ). Objective. Let x ^ p \hat{x}_{p} denote the predicted voxels of patch p p . The model is trained to minimize the mean squared error over masked patches only: ℒ = 1 | M | ​ ∑ p ∈ M 1 512 ​ ‖ x ^ p − x p ‖ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|M|}\sum_{p\in M}\frac{1}{512}\left\lVert\hat{x}_{p}-x_{p}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}, (1) where targets x p x_{p} are defined in the Z-score-normalized intensity space. Because our goal is a robust latent representation of brain structure rather than recovery of absolute voxel intensities, we do not reconstruct the original intensities. Embedding extraction. After pre-training, the decoder is discarded.

We freeze the encoder weights and pass all the patches without any masking. The final embedding is obtained from the [CLS] token, though obtaining the final embedding using mean pooling is also a valid option and is used in other recent foundation models like NeuroJEPA. 3.3 Training During training, we used 8 × 8 × 8 8\times 8\times 8 voxel patches with a random masking ratio of 75%. Fig. 2 illustrates example scans with random masking applied, alongside their reconstruction generated by Brain2Vec and ground truth. Masked Recon. GT (a) CU Masked Recon. GT (b) MCI Masked Recon. GT (c) AD Figure 2 : Brain2Vec reconstruction results (75% random masking) for a representative subject from each cognitive group: (a) CU (Cognitively Unimpaired), (b) MCI (Mild Cognitive Impairment), and (c) AD (Alzheimer’s Disease). Within each panel, columns show the masked input, the Brain2Vec reconstruction (Recon.), and the ground truth (GT); rows show sagittal, coronal, and axial views. Data were split into 80% training, 10% validation, and 10% testing sets, stratified by disease. Given the foundation model nature of this work, the training set was intentionally maximized to expose the model to as much diverse data as possible during pre-training, as broader data coverage is critical for learning generalizable representations. Brain2Vec was trained for 500 epochs with an effective batch size of 64 on two A100 GPUs, using the AdamW optimizer Loshchilov and Hutter (2019) with momentum of β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.95 , a base learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and a cosine annealing scheduler without warm restarts Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) . We applied the linear learning rate scaling rule Goyal et al. (2018) , lr = lr base × B eff / 32 \mathrm{lr}=\mathrm{lr}_{\text{base}}\times B_{\text{eff}}/32 , where B eff = 64 B_{\text{eff}}=64 is the effective batch size, as we trained on two GPUs with a batch size of 32 each.

All scans were skull-stripped using a deep learning–based method and linearly registered to a common atlas space Bashyam et al. (2025) ; Pomponio et al. (2020) . Preprocessed scans were resized to 128 × 128 × 128 128\times 128\times 128 voxels to reduce computational cost. It is important to note that the objective of our training is not precise reconstruction, but rather learning meaningful representations of the input data. To improve generalization, we applied data augmentation using TorchIO Pérez-García et al. (2021) , including RandomBlur ( σ i ∼ υ ⁡ ( 0 , 2 ) \sigma_{i}\sim\upsilon(0,2) ), RandomGamma ( β ∼ υ ⁡ ( − 0.3 , 0.3 ) \beta\sim\upsilon(-0.3,0.3) ), RandomFlip (lateral axis only), RandomNoise (mean=0, std=0), and affine transformations. 3.4 Evaluation The pre-trained Brain2Vec model was evaluated on six downstream tasks including: (i) five classification tasks (CU vs. AD, elevated BMI, diabetes, smoking status and hypertension) and (ii) a brain age prediction task, under two complementary configurations: • Encoder fine-tuning: The pre-trained encoder weights were used as initialization for a Vision Transformer (ViT) applied to a brain age prediction task. This approach preserves the original ViT architecture, allowing the downstream model to leverage the rich structural representations acquired during pre-training. • Feature extraction: MRI scans were passed through the frozen pre-trained encoder to extract 768-dimensional embeddings (Brain2Vec features), which subsequently served as fixed input representations for lightweight downstream models using Support Vector Machines (SVMs). We compared fine-tuning from Brain2Vec pretrained weights against training from random initialization, measuring both final accuracy and convergence speed.

In the feature extraction setting, we compared downstream predictive performance against SPARE-BA, a model trained using segmentation-based regional volumetric features and using features extracted from NeuroJEPA, a state-of-the-art foundation model, providing a direct assessment of Brain2Vec relative to both traditional and more recent neuroimaging feature pipelines. 3.1 Datasets The pre-training dataset comprised 74,425 T1-weighted MRI scans pooled from multiple studies within the iSTAGING consortium Habes et al. We fine-tuned the model on our brain age prediction dataset explained in Sec. 3.1 . In contrast to Brain2Vec model training stage, where maximizing training data sample size was prioritized, a larger proportion of data was used in this validation experiment to ensure robust evaluation of regression performance on the downstream task. Data were partitioned into 60% for training, 30% for validation, and 10% for testing. All training configurations and hyperparameters were kept consistent with those used during the Brain2Vec model training. Results are reported with and without Brain2Vec initialization, enabling a direct assessment of the contribution of transfer learning to downstream regression performance.

As expected from pre-trained initializations, optimization dynamics were markedly improved, with the Brain2Vec-initialized model bypassing the initial plateau within fewer than 10 epochs compared to approximately 50 epochs for the randomly initialized model (Fig. 3 ). This confirms that self-supervised pre-training provides a superior weight initialization that optimizes training efficiency, accelerating convergence. Figure 3 : ViT-BA validation metrics per epoch. Brain2Vec initialization also improved brain age prediction accuracy (Table 2 , Fig. 4 ). The pre-trained model outperformed the randomly initialized baseline across all metrics – Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and R 2 R^{2} – on both the held-out test set and the external IXI dataset Biomedical Image Analysis Group, Imperial College London () , with the performance gap being more pronounced on the latter. The larger improvement on out-of-sample data suggests that pre-training contributes to better generalization across sites. Figure 5 : ViT-BA and Brain2Vec-SVR prediction plots for IXI. 4.2 Feature extraction 4.2.1 Brain age prediction We trained a Support Vector Regressor (SVR) on frozen Brain2Vec encoder embeddings to predict brain age.

The rationale is that an effectively pretrained encoder that captures neuroanatomically relevant structure should enable a simple non-parametric model to generalize effectively to age prediction from fixed embeddings alone, without any backbone fine-tuning. We used 5-fold cross-validation for data splitting, with hyperparameters tuned via Optuna Akiba et al. (2019) using nested 5-fold cross-validation on the training folds, optimizing for R 2 R^{2} score. Splits were randomly sampled. Our results (Table 3 , Fig. 5 ) demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves performance comparable to fully supervised ViT regressors, despite its simplicity, suggesting that Brain2Vec embeddings capture rich structural information relevant to brain aging. Notably, the SVR model trained on Brain2Vec features outperformed SPARE-BA, a validated and established brain age estimation method trained on volumetric features from anatomical segmentation using a pre-defined atlas Habes et al. (2016) , and performed comparable to SVR models trained on NeuroJEPA embeddings. This suggests that Brain2Vec features encode structural information that is at least as informative as anatomically defined, handcrafted regional volume features. We also evaluated the utility of brain age gap (predicted age − - actual age) to capture disease related or risk-factor effects on multiple disease-specific datasets described in Sec. 3.1 . The brain age gap from Brain2Vec-SVR model showed significant group differences in AD (Cohen’s d = 0.94 0.94 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ) and elevated BMI (Cohen’s d = 0.43 0.43 , p < 0.001 p<0.001 ), outperforming ViT-BA model on this measure. Results are reported in supplementary Fig. 8 . Validations on the external IXI dataset were performed using the same SVR models trained in the cross-validation folds, without any additional training or fine-tuning.

This approach was chosen to directly assess the generalization performance of the learned Brain2Vec feature space without any additional model adaptation, consistent with the frozen feature extraction paradigm. The same inference procedure was applied to SPARE-BA models trained on DLMUSE-derived features and NeuroJEPA-SVR trained on NeuroJEPA embeddings, ensuring a fair comparison between approaches under identical conditions. For the IXI inference, we combined predictions from all 5-fold SVR models into an ensemble, as this approach typically yields more robust and stable predictions by averaging out individual model variances. The results of the IXI inference are included in Table 3 and Fig. 5 . The SVR model fitted on Brain2Vec embeddings yielded the best results, confirming that Brain2Vec has learned a generalizable representation of brain morphology that serves as a compact yet informative feature space for efficient downstream tasks. We used 5-fold cross-validation, with hyperparameters tuned via Optuna Akiba et al. (2019) through nested 5-fold cross-validation on each training set, optimizing for F1 score. Splits were stratified by disease or risk-factor. Despite the encoder being trained without any disease supervision, the learned representations yielded strong classification performance across all disease groups, indicating that Brain2Vec captures clinically meaningful morphological structure beyond its explicit training objective. Compared to SPARE models trained on DLMUSE-derived features, our approach outperformed across all tasks in terms of accuracy, AUC, F1 score, recall and precision, except for AD classification, where DLMUSE retained a clear advantage. Compared to NeuroJEPA, Brain2Vec performed better on diabetes and smoking classification, while NeuroJEPA performed better on AD and elevated BMI classification, with comparable results on hypertension (Table 4 ). Brain2Vec reached an accuracy comparable to NeuroJEPA (0.84 vs. 0.83) with substantially higher recall (0.93 vs. 0.76) but lower precision (0.85 vs. 0.99), while NeuroJEPA achieved a higher AUC (0.97 vs. 0.94). Overall, Brain2Vec generalized reasonably well to this independent cohort, although threshold calibration on new cohorts may be needed for all embedding-based models. (2025) .

We assessed Brain2Vec’s interpretability through three complementary strategies: (i) visualizing self-attention maps to examine which spatial regions the model attends to, (ii) correlating latent embeddings with anatomically-defined regions of interest to identify which brain structures drive specific features, and (iii) manipulating latent embeddings and inspecting their effect on reconstructed anatomy to test whether individual features encode monotonic, region-specific changes. We visualized what the model considers important by plotting its self-attention maps (Fig. 6 ). The resulting maps show that different attention heads learn distinct spatial patterns rather than attending uniformly across the entire brain, consistent with findings in other models Caron et al. (2021) . As shown in the attention visualizations, different heads consistently emphasize different anatomical regions across the axial, coronal, and sagittal views. Some heads exhibit relatively localized attention around specific brain structures, whereas others capture more distributed patterns across larger portions of the brain. This diversity suggests that the multi-head self-attention mechanism enables Brain2Vec to encode complementary spatial information, with individual heads potentially capturing different anatomical or contextual characteristics of the input MRI. An important exception is the behavior of heads 0 and 9: across views and samples, these heads frequently assign substantial attention to regions outside the brain, particularly along the image boundaries and background (see Section A.6 ).

This indicates that they are not primarily encoding meaningful brain anatomy and may instead capture image-level or acquisition-related characteristics. Correlation with anatomically defined regions. The latent embeddings of foundation models trained on domain-specific data can be interpreted by quantifying their correlation with anatomically defined regions of interest, particularly those known to be affected by disease. To this end, we computed the Pearson correlation between each individual Brain2Vec latent dimension and each DLMUSE regional volume, together with the mean difference in each latent dimension between CU and AD subjects, in order to identify which dimensions are most strongly associated with which anatomical region. As shown in Fig. 7 , several latent dimensions exhibit strong correlations with specific brain regions, including the ventricles, gray matter, frontal regions, and white matter. Consistent with known neurodegenerative patterns in AD, we observe an inverse relationship between ventricular volume and gray matter, frontal, and white matter volumes. For Brain2Vec, which processes full 3D MRI scans to produce subject-level embeddings, efficient inference is especially important given the large and diverse cohorts it targets. We compared Brain2Vec’s inference time against DLMUSE, which uses an nnU-Net Isensee et al. (2018) to segment the brain and compute ROI volumes from the full 3D input, and against NeuroJEPA, which uses a similar ViT encoder augmented with a Mixture of Experts (MoE) layer Shazeer et al. (2017) at inference time. Benchmarks were conducted on the IXI dataset ( 581 581 scans) using an A40 GPU, as well as single-subject inference on CPU. On GPU, Brain2Vec processed the full IXI cohort in 30 30 seconds ( ≈ 0.05 \approx 0.05 seconds per scan), an ≈ 87 × \approx 87\times speedup over DLMUSE and an ≈ 7 × \approx 7\times speedup over NeuroJEPA. On CPU, Brain2Vec remained ≈ 8 × \approx 8\times faster than DLMUSE, whereas NeuroJEPA was faster than Brain2Vec ( 6.98 6.98 vs. 45.73 45.73 seconds).

This is likely because NeuroJEPA’s sparse MoE layer activates only a subset of its parameters for each input, which reduces sequential computation on CPU. Brain2Vec’s dense ViT encoder, by contrast, benefits more from GPU parallelism. Overall, Brain2Vec offers substantially lower computational cost in GPU-based, cohort-scale settings while maintaining strong predictive performance (Table 6 ). We evaluated Brain2Vec across multiple settings: fine-tuning for brain age prediction, feature extraction for disease classification, external validation on an independent cohort, interpretability analysis, and inference efficiency. We demonstrated that Brain2Vec serves as a versatile dual-purpose framework: (1) accelerating convergence and improving predictive accuracy when fine-tuned as a 3D ViT backbone, and (2) offering a rich, 768-dimensional frozen feature space that is competitive with or superior to both anatomically-derived volumetric features and larger foundation models across a range of disease classification tasks. Beyond predictive performance, we showed that Brain2Vec’s learned representations are anatomically meaningful and interpretable, with generative manipulation of its latent dimensions revealing biologically interpretable, continuous neurodegenerative phenotypes in reconstructed brain space. Our results reveal a consistent trade-off between anatomical segmentations and self-supervised continuous embeddings.

While traditional pipelines like DLMUSE excel at detecting localized structural changes such as volumetric atrophy in Alzheimer’s Disease, they are constrained by fixed anatomical boundaries. Conversely, Brain2Vec representations outperformed DLMUSE on harder classification tasks (e.g., diabetes, smoking, elevated BMI). This suggests that Brain2Vec may be learning representations beyond those captured by standard volumetric features derived from anatomical segmentation. One notable finding of this study is that Brain2Vec-SVR models achieve competitive predictive performance relative to NeuroJEPA, a state-of-the-art foundation model, across several downstream tasks, despite Brain2Vec being pre-trained on ≈ 9.2 × \approx 9.2\times fewer scans ( 74,425 74,425 vs 683,860 683,860 ). We attribute this sample efficiency to the inductive bias of our training objective within the structural MRI domain. At their core, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) like NeuroJEPA, use a context input x x to estimate the embedded state of a target input y y . This process relies on a predictor conditioned on an extra variable z z to account for variability during feature-space prediction. However, in standardized neuroimaging datasets where scans are skull-stripped, atlas-registered, and anatomically aligned, latent representation matching presents a relatively low-variance objective. It is well documented that representation collapse is a concern with JEPA architectures Assran et al. (2023) . In contrast, representation collapse is not a concern with reconstruction-based methods. Generative architectures mask a high percentage of the input and use an encoder to produce latent embeddings z z of the masked input y y and using a decoder, learn to reconstruct the original (unmasked) input x x . This forces the encoder to learn high-fidelity structural priors and inter-regional anatomical dependencies across the entire brain volume.

This dense supervisory signal explains both the model’s high sample efficiency and the strong, explicit alignment observed between Brain2Vec latent dimensions and regional brain volumes (Section 4.3 ). A common critique of deep feature extractors in neuroimaging is their limited interpretability relative to anatomically defined ROI volumes. Through latent manipulation experiments (Section 4.3 ), we provided evidence that Brain2Vec’s latent dimensions can be linked to anatomically meaningful, region-specific effects, offering a step toward addressing this limitation. Progressively shifting latent dimensions along disease-associated vectors produced monotonic, anatomically plausible changes in reconstructed scans, specifically capturing ventricular expansion, and gray and white matter volume decrease. This generative steering provides evidence that the learned latent space encodes coherent, continuous radiological phenotypes rather than uninterpretable noise. Despite being trained on a large and diverse dataset, Brain2Vec has two notable limitations. First, UK Biobank dataset dominates the training data ( ≈ \approx 55%), which may bias learned representations toward its specific acquisition protocol and reduce embedding quality for scans acquired under substantially different conditions. Second, the training cohort is skewed toward older adults (mean age 65.0 65.0 years; fewer than 5 % 5\% of scans from studies with mean age below 45 45 ), which may limit the model’s representational accuracy for younger populations. Users applying Brain2Vec outside its training distribution should take these factors into account. Brain2Vec code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec . Embeddings can be extracted locally via the installable package or through the NiChart cloud platform ( https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com ), which requires no local installation or specialized infrastructure.
